questions_and_answers.question_text: What does the reduplicated form kànkan imply?
What is the alternate form of huòshi?
Write the Chinese for "Tomorrow and (or) the day after are both possible."
How is kànkan best translated into English?

answers.answer_text: As "to have a look" or "to look around."

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I will go to buy some beer or some soft drinks."

answers.answer_text: Wǒ qù mǎi yìdiǎnr píjiǔ huòshi mǎi yìdiǎnr qìshuǐ.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Are you buying beer or soft drinks?"

answers.answer_text: Nǐ mǎi píjiǔ háishi mǎi qìshuǐ?

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which of huòshi and háishi requires the listener to choose?

articles.text:
1. A: Wǒ yě xiǎng dào Nánjīng qù     I would also like to go to Nánjīng
      kànkan.                         to look around.
   B: Nǐ jìhua něitian qù?           What day do you plan to go?
   A: Míngtian huòshi hòutian qù     Tomorrow and (or) the day after are
      dōu kěyi.                       both possible.

Notes on No. 1

Kànkan, "to have a look": In exchange 1, kànkan refers to doing some sight-seeing. The reduplicated verb form implies an indefinite amount of sight-seeing, best translated into English as "to have a look," "to look around."

Huòshi (alternate, huòzhě) is used for "or" when both alternatives are acceptable or possible.

Wǒ qù mǎi yìdiǎnr píjiǔ           I will go to buy some beer or
huòshi mǎi yìdiǎnr qìshuǐ.        some soft drinks.
Tā míngtian huòshi hòutian        Is he coming to see you tomorrow
lái kàn ni ma?                    or the day after? (i.e., some-
                                  time during the next two days)

Háishi is used for "or" when a choice is required between the alternatives.

Nǐ mǎi píjiǔ háishi mǎi           Are you buying beer or (are you
qìshuǐ?                           buying) soft drinks?
Nǐ xǐhuan dàde háishi xǐhuan      Do you like the large one or (do
xiǎode?                           you like) the small one?
